title: The Alphabet, Sounds, and Stress
summary: The thirty-two letters and the order they are filed in; how length is written and why it cannot always be read off the page; the softening i that is not a vowel; the diphthongs; and why stress must be learned with every word.

notes: The letters q, w and x do not belong to the alphabet. They appear only in untranslated foreign names.

Alphabetical order places each diacritical letter immediately after its plain counterpart: a, ą, b, c, č, … i, į, y, … u, ų, ū, v, z, ž. Note that y follows į, not i, and is filed among the i-letters rather than at the end.

rules.heading: The Alphabet
rules.statement: The Lithuanian alphabet has **thirty-two** letters. It is the Latin alphabet with **q**, **w** and **x** removed, and nine letters added by three diacritics: the *nosinė* or hook (**ą ę į ų**), the *paukščiukas* or háček (**č š ž**), and the length marks on **ė** and **ū**. A tenth addition, **y**, carries no diacritic but is a letter in its own right and is alphabetised after **į**, not beside **i**. The order matters because it is the order of every dictionary and index the learner will use.
footnotes: The diacritics are not ornaments. Dropping the hook from **ą** or the bar from **ū** changes the word, and often the grammar: *kąsti* ‘to bite’ is not *kasti* ‘to dig’.
**q, w, x** appear only in unadapted foreign names and formulae; adapted borrowings are respelled (*taksi*, not *taxi*).

rules.heading: Short and Long Vowels
rules.statement: Length distinguishes words, so it must be heard and written. The short vowels are **a e i u**; the long are **ą ę y ū ė o ų į** and long **a** and **e** in stressed syllables. Length is not marked by one consistent device: **y** and **ū** show it by their own shape, **ė** by a letter distinct from **e**, the *nosinė* letters by a hook that no longer stands for nasality, and long **a** and **e** by nothing at all. The learner therefore cannot read length off the page in every case, which is why vocabulary is learned with its stress.

rules.heading: The Nosinė Letters
rules.statement: **ą ę į ų** are called *nosinės* (‘nasal’) after a nasal consonant that was lost centuries ago. They mark **length**, not nasality: nothing is pronounced through the nose. They are worth attention because the hook is very often grammatical — the accusative singular of most nouns ends in one — so a missing hook is usually a missing case ending rather than a slip of the pen.
footnotes: This is why **ą** and long **a** sound alike but are spelled differently: the hook records history and grammar, not a sound.

rules.heading: Consonants Differing from English
rules.statement: Most consonant letters have their expected values. Five do not: **c** is always /ts/, never /k/ or /s/; **č** is /tʃ/; **š** is /ʃ/; **ž** is /ʒ/; and **j** is the glide /j/ of English *yes*, never the affricate of *jam*. Lithuanian **r** is trilled in every position.

rules.heading: The Consonant Digraphs Ch, Dz, Dž
rules.statement: Three pairs of letters spell single sounds: **ch** is a single fricative /x/, **dz** the affricate /dz/, and **dž** the affricate /dʒ/. They are digraphs, not clusters — but they are *not* letters of the alphabet, and a dictionary files *džiaugsmas* under **d**, not between **d** and **e**.

rules.heading: The Softening I
rules.statement: An **i** written between a consonant and a back vowel (**a o u ą ų ū**) is not a vowel: it marks the preceding consonant as **soft** (palatalised) and is itself silent. This is the single most common spelling trap in the language, because the same letter is a full vowel elsewhere. Compare *kiauras* ‘leaky’, where **i** softens the **k** and the vowel is *au*, with *kiaušinis*, where the same holds, against *iš* ‘out of’, where **i** is a vowel because no back vowel follows.

examples.note: soft r; the final -ia is one syllable

footnotes: Before a front vowel (**e ė i y ę į**) a consonant is soft automatically and no **i** is written.

rules.heading: Diphthongs
rules.statement: Lithuanian has the proper diphthongs **ai au ei ie ui uo** and the mixed diphthongs — a short vowel followed by **l m n r** (**al, am, an, ar, el, en, il, im, in, ir, ul, um, un, ur**). Both count as a single long syllable and can carry either tone. **ie** and **uo** are the two that English speakers most often flatten: they are gliding sequences, not the monophthongs of *see* and *saw*.

rules.heading: Spelling and Pronunciation
rules.statement: The orthography is close to phonemic but not a transcription. Two regular departures matter from the start. Voiced obstruents are **devoiced** before a voiceless consonant and at the end of a word, while voiceless ones are voiced before a voiced consonant — yet the spelling keeps the underlying letter, so *daug* is written with **g** and said with /k/. And the softening **i** of ¶6 is written but not sounded. Spelling records the word's identity; pronunciation records its surroundings.

soft č; the i is silent

rules.heading: Stress
rules.statement: Stress is **free** — it may fall on any syllable — and **mobile**: it moves between the forms of one word. *Because* it is mobile, it cannot be predicted from the written word, and a dictionary marks it with three signs: the grave `\` on a short stressed syllable, the acute `´` for the falling tone on a long one, and the tilde `~` for the rising tone. A word is therefore learned with its stress, exactly as a noun is learned with its gender.

examples.note: stress on the stem, and a rising tone

paradigms.caption: The three stress marks
paradigms.footnote: The marks belong to dictionaries and grammars. Running text is written without them.

footnotes: Tone is a property of long syllables only, diphthongs included: a short syllable can be stressed but has no tone to contrast.

sources.citation: Mathiassen, Terje, *A Short Grammar of Lithuanian*. Columbus: Slavica Publishers, 1996.
sources.note: The accentual system and the three marks.

drills.stem: A Lithuanian dictionary is being typeset. Where does **ypatingas** fall relative to **įdomus** and **iš**?
drills.explanation: **y** is a separate letter and is ordered after **į**, which is itself after **i** (¶1). So the run is *iš*, *įdomus*, *ypatingas*. The tempting answers all assume y is filed with i, which is what happens in English indexes and never in Lithuanian ones.
options: before both, since y is a kind of i
between them: iš, ypatingas, įdomus
after both: iš, įdomus, ypatingas
immediately after iš, since y and i are alphabetised together

drills.stem: Which letter is **not** part of the Lithuanian alphabet?
drills.explanation: **q, w, x** were left out and survive only in unadapted foreign names (¶1). The other three are all formed by the three Lithuanian diacritics.
options: ų
w
š
ė

drills.stem: Select every statement about **ą** that is true.
drills.explanation: The *nosinė* marks length; the nasal consonant it records was lost long ago, so nothing is nasalised today (¶3). The hook is frequently the accusative singular ending, which is why a dropped hook is usually a lost case rather than a typo. It is its own letter and is not filed under **a** (¶1).
options: It marks a long vowel.
It is pronounced through the nose in the standard language.
It is very often a grammatical ending rather than part of a stem.
It is alphabetised as a variant of **a**.

drills.stem: **butas** and **būtas** are different words. What distinguishes them?
drills.explanation: *butas* ‘flat’ has short **u**, *būtas* ‘been’ has long **ū** (¶2). Length alone carries the difference, which is why it must be heard as well as written; the pair is not a spelling convention.
options: the position of the stress
the length of the vowel, and nothing else
the tone on the vowel, the length being equal
nothing in speech; only the spelling differs

drills.stem: Match each letter with the value it has in the standard language.
drills.explanation: **ė** is the long close vowel, **y** is long /iː/, **c** is *always* /ts/ and never /k/ or /s/, and **dž** is a single affricate (¶2, ¶4, ¶5). Option B swaps the two affricates, which is the mistake of reading **c** as English *c*; option C swaps the two long vowels; option D gives **c** the value of **dž**. The fricative /x/ belongs to **ch** and is a decoy.

drills.stem: Which numbered rule of this section states that **dž** spells one sound rather than two? Give the paragraph number.
drills.explanation: ¶5 sets out the three digraphs **ch, dz, dž**. ¶4 covers the single consonant letters that differ from English, which is the near miss.

drills.stem: In which of these words is the written **i** silent — a mark of softening rather than a vowel?
drills.explanation: **i** softens when it stands between a consonant and a **back** vowel (¶6). In *čia* and *giria* it does exactly that and is not pronounced. In *iš* and *ilgas* nothing follows it that could make it a softener, so it is the vowel of the syllable.
options: **čia** ‘here’
**iš** ‘out of’
**giria** ‘forest’
**ilgas** ‘long’

drills.stem: Why is no softening **i** written in **ėsti** or **girdėti**, although the consonants before the vowels are soft?
drills.explanation: Softness is written only where it is unpredictable — before a back vowel. Before **e ė i y ę į** a consonant is soft as a matter of course, so no **i** is added (¶6, footnote). The spelling marks what could not be guessed and leaves the rest to the rule.
options: Softening is only written after k and g.
A consonant is soft automatically before a front vowel, so the mark would be redundant.
These words are exceptions listed in the orthography rules.
The consonants in them are in fact hard.

drills.stem: **kalnas** ‘hill’ contains the sequence *al*. What is it?
drills.explanation: A short vowel plus **l m n r** is a *mixed* diphthong: it behaves as one long syllable and can carry tone (¶7). It is not a proper diphthong — those are the six vowel-plus-vowel sequences — but neither is it an ordinary vowel-consonant sequence, which is what the tone tells you.
options: two syllables, since a and l cannot combine
a mixed diphthong, counting as one long syllable
a proper diphthong of the same kind as *au*
a short vowel followed by a consonant, with no special status

drills.stem: Which sequences are proper diphthongs in Lithuanian?
drills.explanation: The proper diphthongs are **ai au ei ie ui uo** (¶7). **io** is not among them: the **i** there is the softener of ¶6 and the vowel is **o**, as in *žodžio*. Hearing *io* as a diphthong is the direct consequence of missing the softening rule.

drills.stem: **daug** is pronounced with a final /k/. Why is it not spelled *dauk*?
drills.explanation: Final devoicing is automatic and therefore predictable, so the orthography keeps the underlying **g** and lets the rule supply the /k/ (¶8). The same principle keeps the **b** of *dirbti* although it is said /p/. Spelling records identity; pronunciation records context.
options: Because the spelling records the word's own consonant, not what its surroundings do to it.
Because /k/ and /g/ are the same sound in Lithuanian.
Because the rule applies only to borrowed words.
Because *dauk* is an older spelling now abandoned.

drills.stem: *kalbà* and *kal̃bos* are two forms of one noun, stressed differently. What does this show?
drills.explanation: Stress is free *and* mobile: it may sit on any syllable, and it shifts from one form of a word to another (¶9). That mobility is exactly why stress cannot be read off the page and must be learned with the word.
options: that the two forms belong to different words
that Lithuanian stress is mobile, moving between the forms of a word
that the plural is always stressed on the stem
that the stress mark is optional in both

drills.stem: A dictionary gives *kal̃bos* with a tilde. What does the tilde tell you that a grave accent could not?
drills.explanation: All three marks show stress; they differ in what else they encode. The grave stands on a **short** stressed syllable, which has no tone to contrast; the tilde and the acute distinguish rising from falling tone on a **long** one (¶9). So the tilde says *long, and rising*.
options: that the syllable is stressed
that the syllable is long and carries the rising tone
that the stress moves in other forms of the word
that the vowel is nasal in origin

drills.stem: Of the four words **várna**, **kalbà**, **namè**, **kal̃bos**, how many carry a mark that can only stand on a long syllable?
drills.explanation: The acute and the tilde require a long syllable; the grave requires a short one (¶9). *várna* (acute) and *kal̃bos* (tilde) are the two. *kalbà* and *namè* both take the grave, so their stressed syllables are short and toneless.

drills.stem: **žodžio** is the genitive of *žodis*. Which statements about the written form are correct?
drills.explanation: Three rules meet in one word. **dž** is a digraph for one sound (¶5) but is not a letter, so it files under **d** (¶1, ¶5). The **i** stands between a consonant and the back vowel **o**, so it softens and is silent (¶6) — there is no diphthong *io* (¶7).
options: **dž** here spells a single affricate.
The **i** before **o** is a vowel forming a diphthong *io*.
The **i** before **o** is silent and marks **dž** as soft.
**dž** is alphabetised between **d** and **e**.

drills.stem: A learner writes *kasti* for ‘to bite’ and *ačiu* for ‘thank you’. What single principle have both errors broken?
drills.explanation: *kąsti* ‘to bite’ and *kasti* ‘to dig’ are separate words distinguished by the hook alone (¶1, ¶3); *ačiū* has a long **ū** (¶2). Neither mark is decoration: one carries the vowel's length, the other very often carries a grammatical ending.
options: Both letters are optional in careful handwriting.
A diacritic is part of the letter: dropping it produces a different letter, and often a different word or a different case.
Both words are irregular and simply have to be memorised.
Both errors are pronunciations, not spellings.

drills.stem: Each word below is misspelled in one respect. Match it with the rule its spelling breaks.
drills.explanation: *ylgas* gives a short **i** the long letter **y**; *ča* drops the softening **i** required before the back vowel **a**; *dauk* spells the devoicing instead of the underlying **g**; *abecele* drops the length letters **ė**, which is again ¶2 — so ¶2 is used twice and ¶9 not at all. The distractors all assume each rule is used exactly once, which is the habit this item is built to break.
columnII: ¶2 — length is written with the letter that carries it
¶6 — softening before a back vowel must be written
¶9 — stress is not marked in running text

drills.title: Pirmoji pamoka
drills.passage:
JONAS. Labas! Kaip tavo vardas?
RŪTA. Labas. Aš esu Rūta. O tu?
JONAS. Aš Jonas. Rūta, kas tai?
RŪTA. Tai abėcėlė. Lietuvių kalba turi trisdešimt dvi raides.
JONAS. O kas yra „ą“?
RŪTA. Tai balsė. Ji ilga. Nosinė nėra nosinis garsas — tik ilgas.
JONAS. Ačiū!
RŪTA. Prašom.

questions.stem: Kiek raidžių turi lietuvių kalba, pasak Rūtos?
questions.explanation: Rūta says *Lietuvių kalba turi trisdešimt dvi raides.* Twenty-six is the basic Latin alphabet, which is what Lithuanian starts from and adds to.
options: dvidešimt šešias
dvidešimt devynias
trisdešimt dvi
trisdešimt tris

questions.explanation: Jonas asks *O kas yra „ą“?* and Rūta answers. The labels make the turns followable: Jonas is the one who does not yet know the alphabet.
options: Jonas
Rūta
mokytojas
niekas

questions.stem: What does Rūta say the hook on **ą** indicates?
questions.explanation: *Nosinė nėra nosinis garsas — tik ilgas*: the hook marks length, not nasality, which is ¶3 put into the speaker's own words.
options: that the vowel is nasal
that the vowel is long
that the syllable is stressed
that the letter is foreign

questions.stem: In **raides**, the final syllable is *-des*. Is the **d** soft?
questions.explanation: Before a front vowel a consonant is soft as a matter of course and nothing is written (¶6, footnote). The **i** of *raidės* belongs to the diphthong *ai*, not to the last syllable, so answer B misidentifies which vowel is doing the work.
options: Yes — it stands before the front vowel **e**, so softness is automatic and unwritten.
Yes — the **i** of *raides* softens it.
No — **d** is never soft in Lithuanian.
No — softness would require a written **i**.

questions.stem: The dialogue writes **Ačiū** with a long **ū** and a soft **č**. If a learner wrote *Aciu*, how many of the section's rules would the spelling break?
questions.explanation: *Aciu* loses the bar on **ū** (¶2) and the háček on **č** (¶1, ¶4), turning /tʃ/ into /ts/. The **i** is still written, so the softening rule ¶6 is not broken — which is what separates this from the tempting answer D.
options: one — only the length mark
two — the length of **ū** and the softening **i**
two — the length of **ū** and the háček on **č**
three — length, softening, and the háček

sources.note: A first-meeting dialogue; the grammar it leans on is ¶1–¶6.

sources.citation: Ambrazas, Vytautas (ed.), *Lithuanian Grammar*. Vilnius: Baltos lankos, 1997.
sources.note: The letter inventory and the value of the nosinė.

drills.translation: — Hello! What is your name? — Hello. I am Rūta. And you? — I'm Jonas. Rūta, what is this? — That is the alphabet. Lithuanian has thirty-two letters. — And what is “ą”? — It is a vowel. It is long. The nosinė is not a nasal sound — only a long one. — Thank you! — You're welcome.
